--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Previous studies have shown that birth order is an important predictor of later life health as well as socioeconomic attainment. In this study, we examine the relationship between birth order and hospitalization for alcohol and narcotics use in Sweden.
[METHODS]: We study the relationship between birth order and hospitalization related to alcohol and narcotics use before and after the age of 20 using Swedish register data for cohorts born 1987-1994. We apply Cox proportional hazard models and use sibling fixed effects, eliminating confounding by factors shared by the siblings.
[RESULTS]: Before age 20 we find that later born siblings are hospitalized for alcohol use at a higher rate than first-borns, and there is a monotonic increase in the hazard of hospitalization with increasing birth order. Second-borns are hospitalized at a rate 47% higher than first-borns, and third-borns at a rate 65% higher. Similar patterns are observed for hospitalization for narcotics use. After age 20 the pattern is similar, but the association is weaker. These patterns are consistent across various sibling group sizes.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Later born siblings are more likely to be hospitalized for both alcohol and narcotics use in Sweden. key_findings.finding: The directly relevant Swedish population-based study is Kendler et al., “Birth order and hospitalization for alcohol and narcotics use in Sweden” (Drug and Alcohol Dependence, 2016; PMID 27507659). It used Swedish register data for birth cohorts 1987–1994, modeled birth order with Cox proportional-hazards models, and used sibling fixed effects to control for factors shared by siblings.

In the 2016 study, exposure was later birth order relative to first-born siblings (with monotonic comparisons by sibling position). Before age 20, alcohol-related hospitalization hazards were 47% higher for second-borns versus first-borns (HR approximately 1.47) and 65% higher for third-borns versus first-borns (HR approximately 1.65); the abstract does not report 95% confidence intervals. Similar increasing patterns were reported for narcotics-related hospitalization, but the abstract gives no narcotics-specific point estimates or confidence intervals. After age 20, associations remained directionally similar but were weaker.

A later Swedish sibling/cohort study, “Birth order and health events attributable to alcohol and narcotics in midlife” (SSM–Population Health, 2022; PMID 36091296), followed a national 1953 birth cohort and siblings from ages 30–55. Outcomes were alcohol- or narcotics-attributable hospitalization or death, identified from the Swedish National Patient and Cause of Death Registers. It estimated between-family associations and within-family/family-type fixed-effects models; bivariate associations increased with birth order for both outcomes, but disappeared after adjustment for familial-background characteristics in all models.
